questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I always really liked traveling to England and wanted to experience what it would be like to live there. I chose York specifically because I thought both the city as well as Yorkshire in general looked really pretty.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I couldn't have had a better semester abroad. York is such a lovely city :)

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. The university sent a bunch of emails with information, and the visiting students team also hosted a pre-arrival Zoom meeting where we were told everything we would need to know before arriving.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I signed up for the university's airport collection service, so when I arrived in Manchester, I was picked up at the airport and driven all the way to the university. At the university there were volunteers who showed us around and helped us get checked into our student accommodation. Throughout the welcome week there were also a bunch of talks and events to help us get settled.
The visiting students team also hosted a few socials during the semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Everyone at the university is really friendly and helpful. If you have any issues, just contact them. I originally misunderstood the English requirements and didn't know that the Politics course specifically requires visiting students to provide an IELTS-test. I called and emailed with the university, and in the end they accepted my English A from STX combined with a language document from KU, and I was able to save a lot of time and money by not having to take the IELTS-test.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: All undergraduate visiting students are guaranteed on-campus housing, so not having to stress about that was really nice. There are both rooms with shared and private bathrooms as well as with and without catering. You can also send the accommodation team an email with your preferences, and then they'll try to account for that when assigning your room.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: All rooms had shared kitchens, and then some housing was also catered. My accommodation was catered, so I had breakfast and dinner at my college Monday-Friday, which was very convenient.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I sent the university an email with my housing preferences and got my first priority which was in Fairfax House. However, I would probably have chosen differently if I had known beforehand that I would be living with mainly British 18-year-old first-year students, while the majority of the other exchange students lived in a different building. Fairfax House was cheap, close to the city, and has catering during the week, which was all really nice. However, the building is pretty run-down, and it was kind of a running joke with my friends that there was always something at Fairfax that wasn’t working. A lot of the first-years living there also still needed to learn how to clean up after themselves and not yell in the hallways in the middle of the night. I think if you want something cheap it’s fine, but if you want to have more of a social experience where you live, I would pay the extra money and ask to be put in a building with other exchange students (from what I know, we were only three exchange students out of the 80+ people living in Fairfax House). During my semester most of the exchange students lived in Derwent block P. Their rent was pretty expensive, but the facilities are also really nice, since the building is newly renovated, and their flats were all really social.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think it’s really nice that they provide housing, but my housing specifically was a bit of a mixed experience. If you want something cheap, I would probably still pick Fairfax House, as it’s closer to the city than the other cheap buildings, but just be aware that the walls are very thin, and most of your housemates will probably be 18.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: A few weeks after completing my online enrollment and getting my York-email address, I was contacted by the Politics department who asked for my module choices. I sent them an email with the modules I wished to take, and then they made sure I was registered for those modules.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I was told I could contact the department if I had any questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successful. I sent them a list of three modules, and then they registered me for those three modules.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don’t worry if they don’t tell you that you got the modules you asked for. I was confused at first, because I never got an email back, but then I saw on the website that the registration was already in the system, they just didn’t email to let me know that it had gone through.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took a first-year module, a second-year module, and a third-year module. The second and third-year modules felt similar to the level of difficulty at KU, but the first-year module was very easy and a bit like being back in Gymnasiet.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The seminar groups are a lot smaller - about 10-12 people per seminar group. I was surprised by how much I liked having a smaller group. It meant that instead of the same couple of people raising their hand, everyone was engaged in the discussions. There was also a lot more interaction with the lecturers as they were often also the ones teaching during the seminars.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Introduction to Comparative Politics - POL00013C (10 ECTS)
European Union Politics - POL00079I (10 ECTS)
Politics of Peace after Civil War - POL00068H (10 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I combined Introduction to Comparative Politics and Politics of Peace after Civil War to get DAK3 approved and took European Union Politics as EP. European Union Politics and Politics of Peace after Civil War were both really interesting. Introduction to Comparative Politics I wouldn’t have taken if I didn’t need to in order to get DAK3 approved. It was like DAK1, DAK2, and DAK3 combined into a single course, so a lot of the things we covered, I had already learned at KU.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of expenses in the first month buying stuff for my room and the kitchen. I really hated the mattress, so I ended up ordering a mattress topper from Jysk. It was money I did not expect to spend, but I really did not regret it as I slept very comfortably for the rest of the semester and was able to bring it home to Denmark in a vacuum bag.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport. I thought I would be taking the bus into the city, but instead I just walked everywhere.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn’t end top joining any societies or sports, but some of my friends did, and they really liked it.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They had a lot of different sports and societies. Whatever hobby you have, they probably have a society for it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I didn’t end up joining any societies, but I would probably just recommend going to the welcome fair and seeing if anything interests you.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Travel! York is the perfect location for a bunch of different day-trips. A few of the places I went and really loved were the Lake District, Knaresborough, Staithes, Robin Hood’s Bay, Whitby, and Durham. Yorkshire also has a lot of great spots for hiking. For longer trips I can also recommend going to London and Edinburgh.
Also - buy a railcard! It saves you a lot of money on train tickets.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy. British culture is relatively similar to Danish culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
In England they start university at 18, so all the local students were very young. I small-talked with the people I had seminars with as well as with some of my housemates, but other than that I didn’t really have that much contact with the British students. Pretty much all my friends were other exchange students.
I did enter the university’s “buddy scheme”, where they matched new international students with student volunteers, and made friends with the buddy I was assigned. However, most of the students that sign up to be a buddy are second or third-year international students that study full-time in York.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The age gap made it difficult to get to know that many British people, but I just spent my time with the other exchange students instead, so it wasn’t really that big of a problem.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness. People in England, especially in the North, are a lot more friendly and less reserved towards strangers than in Denmark.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. York is such a lovely city! I had never been there before going on exchange, and it truly exceeded all my expectations. The streets are very charming and filled with cute cafes and shops. I can also really recommend buying a 1£ coffee from Pret and taking a walk in the museum gardens or by the river. The Minster Gate Bookshop also has a lot of really cheap books. Also, visiting the Minster is free for all York residents. You have to pay to go up into the tower, but the view from there is really nice. The city walls have some great views as well. In general, I found the city to be a really nice size. There were plenty of things to do, but it was also small enough that you could just walk instead of having to take public transport.
2. The campus looks a lot nicer in person than in pictures. I thought it would be kind of ugly, because a lot of the buildings aren’t that pretty, but the lakes, trees, and wildlife make it feel like you’re walking through a park. Especially in autumn, it was very pretty.
3. Just reach out to the university if you have any issues. They are really nice and always happy to help.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Buy a railcard and download the UniDays app - it has a bunch of different student discounts.
Also, when the university invites you to a visa registration event, you still have to go, even if you’re not there on a visa. We were given a bit of conflicting information about it, but you just have to book a time slot and show them your ETA instead of a visa.
The bagels at the library café are also really good :)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Moving to a different country all by myself. Building a whole life in a different country and meeting people from all over the world was such a fun and fulfilling experience.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The age gap between me and my housemates. I was lucky that my room was next to another exchange student who was my age, but everyone else in the house was significantly younger than us. I think it might have been less of an issue, if a lot of them weren’t also pretty inconsiderate when it came to cleaning up after themselves and quieting down at night.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
